jazz_1925.csv.note: Ethel Waters recorded Dinah on October 20, 1925 for Columbia 487-D, billed with her Plantation Orchestra. It reached number 2 in 1926. Sweet Georgia Brown reached number 6 in 1925. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1926.csv.note: Ethel Waters recorded I'm Coming Virginia in September 1926. It reached number 10 in 1927.

jazz_1927.csv.note: East St. Louis Toodle-Oo was first recorded on November 29, 1926. The record that charted, Columbia 953, entered the pop list on July 30, 1927, during Ellington's first Cotton Club residency. Black and Tan Fantasy was recorded on April 7, 1927 and issued on Brunswick 3526. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1928.csv.note: The Mooche was recorded on October 1, 1928 and issued on OKeh 8623, with Baby Cox singing. It entered the pop list on December 29, 1928.

jazz_1929.csv.note: Am I Blue? and Birmingham Bertha were recorded on May 14, 1929 for Columbia 1837-D and sung in the film On with the Show!. Am I Blue? reached number 1. Fats Waller's piano record of Ain't Misbehavin', which he wrote with Andy Razaf and Harry Brooks, was recorded on August 2, 1929 and issued that year. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1930.csv.note: Mood Indigo was issued on December 11, 1930 as Dreamy Blues, Brunswick 4952. The company changed the title to Mood Indigo in March 1931. Filed under the title it is known by, in the year the record came out.

jazz_1932.csv.note: It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing) was recorded on February 2, 1932 for Brunswick 6265, with Ivie Anderson singing. On December 22, 1932 Ethel Waters recorded I Can't Give You Anything but Love with Duke Ellington and his orchestra, issued on Brunswick 6517. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1933.csv.note: Ethel Waters introduced Stormy Weather at the Cotton Club and recorded it on May 3, 1933 for Brunswick 6564. It reached number 1. Heat Wave, from Irving Berlin's As Thousands Cheer, was recorded on October 10, 1933. Underneath the Harlem Moon is her song in the 1933 short Rufus Jones for President. It was not issued as a 78. Sophisticated Lady was recorded on May 16, 1933 for Brunswick 6600. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1934.csv.note: Solitude was recorded on January 10, 1934 and issued on Victor 24755. Honeysuckle Rose, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, was recorded on November 7, 1934 and issued on Victor 24826 on December 9, 1934. Waller wrote it with Andy Razaf.

jazz_1935.csv.note: In a Sentimental Mood was recorded on April 30, 1935 and issued on Brunswick 7461. What a Little Moonlight Can Do was recorded on July 2, 1935 and issued on Brunswick 7498. The label billed Teddy Wilson and His Orchestra, with Billie Holiday singing. I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, was issued on May 29, 1935. Truckin' was a number 1 for him the same year. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1936.csv.note: Summertime, Billie Holiday, reached number 12 in 1936. These Foolish Things (Remind Me of You) reached number 5 the same year. It's a Sin to Tell a Lie, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, was recorded on June 5, 1936 and issued on Victor 25342 on June 17. It spent 12 weeks at number 1. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1938.csv.note: I'm Gonna Lock My Heart, Billie Holiday, reached number 2 in 1938. A-Tisket, A-Tasket, Ella Fitzgerald with Chick Webb and His Orchestra, Decca 1840, was number 1. Two Sleepy People, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, was recorded on October 13, 1938 for Bluebird and spent 11 weeks at number 1. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1937.csv.note: The second edition of the Cotton Club Parade of 1937 billed Ethel Waters with Duke Ellington. Caravan, written by Juan Tizol, was recorded by Ellington's full orchestra on May 14, 1937. Barney Bigard and His Jazzopators, with Ellington at the piano, had made the first record of it on December 19, 1936. The Joint Is Jumpin', Fats Waller and His Rhythm, was issued on Victor 25689 in 1937.

jazz_1939.csv.note: Billie Holiday recorded Strange Fruit and Fine and Mellow on April 20, 1939. Commodore issued them together that month. Lewis Allan wrote Strange Fruit. Undecided, Ella Fitzgerald with Chick Webb and His Orchestra, reached number 8 in 1939. Your Feet's Too Big, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, was recorded on November 3, 1939 and issued that month on Bluebird B-10500. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1940.csv.note: Ko-Ko was recorded on March 6, 1940 and issued on Victor 26577. Taking a Chance on Love is from Cabin in the Sky, which opened on October 25, 1940. Waters recorded it on November 7, 1940 for Liberty Music Shop. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1941.csv.note: Take the A Train, written by Billy Strayhorn, was recorded on February 15, 1941 and issued on Victor 27380. Ethel Waters recorded Georgia on My Mind on August 15, 1939 with Eddie Mallory's orchestra. Bluebird B-11028 was released on January 31, 1941. Ray Charles's 1960 record stays in soul for 1960. Count Basie and His Orchestra recorded Goin' to Chicago Blues, with Jimmy Rushing, on April 10, 1941. OKeh 6244 was issued that year. God Bless the Child, which Billie Holiday wrote with Arthur Herzog Jr., was recorded on May 9, 1941 and issued on OKeh 6270. Gloomy Sunday was recorded on August 7, 1941 and issued on OKeh 6451. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1942.csv.note: Trav'lin' Light was issued in 1942 under Paul Whiteman and His Orchestra, with Billie Holiday singing. It reached number 1 on the R&B chart.

jazz_1944.csv.note: Lover Man (Oh, Where Can You Be?) was recorded on October 4, 1944 and issued on Decca 23391 that year. It reached the pop and R&B charts in 1945. I'm Making Believe and Into Each Life Some Rain Must Fall, Ella Fitzgerald with the Ink Spots, were issued together on Decca 23356 in October 1944. Both reached number 1. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1945.csv.note: It's Only a Paper Moon, Ella Fitzgerald with the Delta Rhythm Boys, reached number 9 in 1945 and number 4 on the R&B chart. I'm Beginning to See the Light, with the Ink Spots, reached number 5. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1946.csv.note: Good Morning Heartache was recorded on January 22, 1946 and issued on Decca 23676. Don't Explain, which Billie Holiday wrote with Arthur Herzog Jr., was issued the same year. Stone Cold Dead in the Market (He Had It Coming), Ella Fitzgerald with Louis Jordan, Decca 23546, June 1946, reached number 1 on the R&B chart. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1948.csv.note: How High the Moon was recorded on December 20, 1947 and issued on Decca 24387 in April 1948. This is the scat record. A live single of it charted in 1960.

jazz_1949.csv.note: Baby, It's Cold Outside, Ella Fitzgerald with Louis Jordan, reached number 9 in 1949 and number 6 on the R&B chart.

jazz_1959.csv.note: I Loves You, Porgy was issued by Bethlehem in June 1959 and reached number 18 on the pop chart and number 2 on the R&B chart. My Baby Just Cares for Me is from the same album, Little Girl Blue, recorded in December 1957. A 1987 reissue of that recording reached number 5 in Britain. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1960.csv.note: Mack the Knife is from Ella in Berlin, recorded on February 13, 1960. The single reached number 27 on the pop chart and number 6 on the R&B chart.

jazz_1964.csv.note: Mississippi Goddam, Philips, July 1964, is from Nina Simone in Concert. She wrote it after the killing of Medgar Evers and the Birmingham church bombing. Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood was issued in October 1964. The order is a listening order, not a chart rank.

jazz_1965.csv.note: I Put a Spell on You was issued by Philips in 1965 and reached number 23 on the R&B chart. Feeling Good is on the same album, recorded in January 1965. It was not a single until 1994, when it reached number 40 in Britain. The old mock chart for this year was removed.

jazz_1968.csv.note: Ain't Got No, I Got Life, from the album 'Nuff Said, was issued in 1968. It reached number 2 in Britain and number 1 in the Netherlands.

jazz_1970.csv.note: To Be Young, Gifted and Black was recorded at Philharmonic Hall on October 26, 1969 and issued in 1970 on the album Black Gold. The single reached number 8 on the R&B chart. Weldon Irvine wrote the lyric. Nina Simone wrote the music.

jazz_1953.csv.note: Satin Doll was recorded on April 6, 1953 at Ellington's first Capitol session and issued on Capitol 2458. It reached number 27. Billy Strayhorn finished the tune from an Ellington sketch. Johnny Mercer's lyric came later.
